summary: Spherical and irregular microplastics both accumulated in the digestive system of sheepshead minnow, causing intestinal distention and reactive oxygen species.
Review of microplastic uptake, accumulation and mechanistic toxicity across trophic levels, including energy metabolism and liver physiology changes.
Co-exposure to microplastic and venlafaxine raised liver superoxide dismutase and malondialdehyde in loach and delayed drug metabolism.
Polystyrene particles of 0.5 micrometres accumulated in gill, liver and gut of juvenile crabs, slowed growth and induced hepatopancreatic oxidative stress.
Polystyrene microplastics first inhibited then enhanced growth of the alga Chlorella pyrenoidosa; a phytoplankton growth study.
Forty-five days of dietary exposure to six virgin microplastic types did not induce stress or pathology in gilt-head seabream, though particles lodged in some livers.
Nanopolystyrene at environmentally relevant concentrations enhanced titanium dioxide nanoparticle toxicity in nematodes, reducing locomotion and raising intestinal reactive oxygen species.
In nematodes with a defective intestinal barrier, nanopolystyrene translocated to target organs and dysregulated oxidative stress genes through Nrf signalling.
Polystyrene nanoparticles passed from exposed adult zebrafish to their offspring and altered the antioxidant system without major physiological disturbance.
Laser-ablated PET nanoplastics were internalised in endolysosomes of human intestinal epithelial cells and crossed a model gut barrier.
Polyethylene microplastic beads alone altered catalase and glutathione peroxidase activity in blue mussel gill and digestive gland.
Bacterial communities colonising microplastics in the Bay of Brest were sequenced by polymer type and size; environmental microbiology.
Polystyrene nano and microplastics inhibited growth and nitrogen conversion in a marine bacterium; an ecological function study.
Polystyrene microplastics accumulated in jacopever gills and intestine, altered feeding and swimming and caused gallbladder and liver histopathology.
Microplastics and mercury altered filtration rate and biochemical biomarkers in a freshwater bivalve, with effects persisting after six recovery days.
Six weeks of 5 micrometre polystyrene microplastics reduced intestinal mucus, damaged barrier function and caused dysbiosis and metabolic disorder in mice.
Anthropogenic particles counted in the stomachs and livers of wild freshwater chub from the Paris area; a contamination survey.
Nanosized beads accumulated more than microsized ones in a marine rotifer, damaged lipid membranes and disrupted multixenobiotic resistance transporters.
Polystyrene microplastics with cadmium induced oxidative stress and altered innate immune markers in juvenile discus fish over 30 days.
Desorption of hydrophobic organic chemicals from polyethylene film into artificial gut fluid was measured to model microplastic-bound intake by fish.
Low density polyethylene microplastics in soil altered oxidative stress and energy metabolism biomarkers in earthworms above 250 mg per kg.
Microplastic fibres and fragments identified in the intestines of fish from two Indian landing sites; an occurrence survey.
Polystyrene nanoplastic was ingested by Daphnia pulex and reduced growth and reproduction while inducing oxidative stress and heat shock gene expression.
Polymethyl methacrylate nanoplastics of about 45 nm raised lipid metabolism gene expression and lowered plasma esterase activity in sea bass.
Systematic review weighing evidence for microplastic harm, finding measured environmental concentrations far below those that affect biological endpoints.
